competency_fulfillment.rationale: The three cases in each item genuinely eliminate every foil offered, which is what makes the induction sound. Seed 44 gives 'a 2 by 2 square takes 4 tiles, a 3 by 3 square takes 9 tiles, and a 5 by 5 square takes 25 tiles': the foil 'side + side' fits the first case exactly (2 + 2 makes 4) and only dies at the second (3 + 3 is 6, not 9), so a pupil cannot stop after one case. Seed 50's triple 9, 16, 25 likewise lets '4 × side' match the 4 by 4 case before the 3 by 3 case kills it, leaving 'side × side' as the sole survivor.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both formulas the competency names are derived, and in balanced numbers: seven square items keyed to 'side × side' (seeds 44, 45, 50, 500, 501, 502, 600) and eight rectangle items keyed to 'length × width' (seeds 42, 43, 46, 601, 602, 604, 605, 606). Seed 600's 'a 2 by 2 square takes 4 tiles, a 4 by 4 square takes 16 tiles, and a 5 by 5 square takes 25 tiles' and seed 46's 'a 6 by 5 rectangle takes 30 tiles, a 7 by 5 rectangle takes 35 tiles, and an 8 by 5 rectangle takes 40 tiles' show the two derivations side by side.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The rules are offered in ordinary words rather than algebra, so seed 42's choice among 'length + width', 'length + length', 'length × width' and 'length + width + length + width' asks a Grade 3 pupil to test arithmetic on given counts, not to manipulate symbols. The arithmetic stays inside the tables: the largest case anywhere is seed 604's 'a 10 by 4 rectangle takes 40 tiles', and every count is supplied in the stem so no pupil has to tile anything mentally before comparing rules.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: All fifteen samples run one sentence frame ending 'Which rule always gives the number of tiles?', with only mcq and cloze appearing and no pictorial array item at all. Worse, the case triples repeat verbatim: seeds 50, 500 and 501 all present 'a 3 by 3 square takes 9 tiles, a 4 by 4 square takes 16 tiles, and a 5 by 5 square takes 25 tiles', and seeds 44 and 502 are likewise identical, so fifteen samples collapse to eleven distinct items. Six of the eight rectangle items also pin the second dimension at four, as in seed 602's 'a 6 by 4 rectangle takes 24 tiles, a 7 by 4 rectangle takes 28 tiles, and an 8 by 4 rectangle takes 32 tiles', so the evidence a pupil sees never once varies the width.

competency_alignment.rationale: The question asked is exactly the derivation the competency calls for: cases first, rule second, keyed to 'length × width' and 'side × side'. The rectangle foils are properly excluded too, including the near-miss at seed 601 'a 2 by 4 rectangle takes 8 tiles', where reading length as the longer side would make 'length + length' fit until the next case 'a 6 by 4 rectangle takes 24 tiles' refutes it, while the perimeter foil 'length + width + length + width' gives 12 against the stated 8. Nothing asks for an area value in standard units, which would overshoot this node.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Dimensions run 2 to 10 and tile counts 4 to 40, so seed 42's 'a 3 by 4 rectangle takes 12 tiles, a 6 by 4 rectangle takes 24 tiles, and a 9 by 4 rectangle takes 36 tiles' asks a pupil only to check products already inside the Grade 3 tables. The squares stop at 'a 5 by 5 square takes 25 tiles' (seed 45), well short of any two-digit-by-two-digit demand.
